extracted.intended_audience: researchers and analysts conducting systematic reviews and meta-analyses
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for detecting, testing, adjusting for, and minimising publication (and related) biases in systematic reviews and meta-analyses, including visual (funnel plot), statistical, modelling, and procedural methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Funnel plot usefulness and limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: For a funnel plot to be useful there needs to be a range of studies with varying sizes. The funnel plot is an informal and subjective method for assessing potential small-study effect; different people may interpret the same plot differently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Visual impression can change depending on which measure of trial magnitude (SE, variance, sample size, etc.) or which outcome scale (risk difference, relative risk, odds ratio) is used. A symmetrical funnel plot cannot exclude publication bias; a skewed plot may arise by chance. Use funnel plots only as an informal, exploratory tool and interpret cautiously.

rubrics_metrics.name: Causes of funnel plot asymmetry (alternative explanations)
rubrics_metrics.description: A skewed funnel plot may be caused by factors other than publication bias.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Possible sources include different intensity of intervention, differences in underlying risk, poor methodological design of small studies, inadequate analysis, fraud, choice of effect measure, clinical heterogeneity, and chance. Investigate clinical or methodological heterogeneity (e.g. subgroup differences such as baseline risk) before attributing asymmetry to publication bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: General limitations of statistical tests for funnel plot asymmetry
rubrics_metrics.description: All proposed tests have important limitations, including low statistical power to identify funnel plot asymmetry when it exists, and inflated rates of type I error when funnel plot asymmetry does not exist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Performance is particularly poor when between-study heterogeneity is large. Different tests may lead to different conclusions. Use tests as exploratory, not definitive proof of bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ioannidis & Trikalinos criteria for appropriateness of funnel plot tests
rubrics_metrics.description: Statistical tests for funnel plot asymmetry may be appropriate only if the following four criteria are met:
rubrics_metrics.guidance: • no significant heterogeneity (I2 < 50%); • 10 or more studies (with statistically significant results in at least one study); • ratio of the maximal to minimal variance across studies > 4. Note these criteria are not based on convincing empirical evidence and few meta-analyses meet them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cochrane Handbook recommendations for use of funnel-plot tests
rubrics_metrics.description: Summarised recommendations about when and how to use statistical tests for funnel plot asymmetry from the updated Cochrane Handbook.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: • Do not use tests in meta-analyses with fewer than 10 studies. • Studies should have different sizes (though the sufficient difference is unclear). • Egger’s test: use for continuous outcomes measured by mean differences. • For dichotomous outcomes measured by odds ratio: use Harbord, Peters or Rucker tests in the absence of significant heterogeneity (ι2 < 0.1). • Use arcsine random-effect regression when both treatment effect and heterogeneity are large (e.g. ι2 > 0.1). • Specify funnel-plot testing strategy in advance and use only one test. • Other tests in Table 2 are not recommended mainly because of low power or lack of statistical evaluation. Evidence is limited for RR/RD and for standardised mean differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Begg and Mazumdar rank correlation test
rubrics_metrics.description: Rank correlation test of the association between standardised effect size and its variance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nonparametric rank-based approach. Suffers from lack of power; a non-significant result does not rule out funnel plot asymmetry, especially when number of studies is small.

rubrics_metrics.name: Egger's linear regression test
rubrics_metrics.description: Regression of the standard normal deviate (ln OR divided by its SE) against the estimate’s precision (inverse of SE), weighted by the inverse of the variance; the intercept measures funnel plot asymmetry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: More powerful than Begg’s test but biased for binary data due to intrinsic association of SND and precision. Has high false-positive rates, particularly when the treatment effect and/or number of studies is large. Use cautiously and prefer only where appropriate (e.g., continuous mean differences per Cochrane guidance).

rubrics_metrics.name: Macaskill's test
rubrics_metrics.description: Linear regression of the estimated treatment effects (dependent variable) and corresponding sample size (Nt), weighted by the inverse of the variance of the logit of the pooled proportion (using the marginal total).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Developed to reduce correlation between weight and treatment effect; statistical power of the test is low.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deeks' method (Galbraith radial plot regression)
rubrics_metrics.description: Method based on a regression analysis of Galbraith's radial plot where the SND is regressed against precision; interpretation of the intercept alpha is similar to Egger’s method.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Power and type I error have not been properly investigated for some settings; limited evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harbord modified Egger test
rubrics_metrics.description: Modified Egger’s test: regression of Z/√V against √V, where Z is the efficient score and V the score variance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Developed for binary outcomes; with large heterogeneity (e.g. ι2 > 0.1) the test can have problems similar to Egger’s (high false-positive and low power).

rubrics_metrics.name: Peters linear regression test
rubrics_metrics.description: Linear regression of estimated treatment effect against 1/√Nt; weights used as in Macaskill’s test.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Superior to Egger’s in terms of more appropriate type I error rates for some binary-data settings. As with other tests, power is low when heterogeneity is large.

rubrics_metrics.name: Schwarzer et al. rank-correlation test for sparse 2x2 tables
rubrics_metrics.description: Rank correlation test based on observed and expected cell frequencies, and the variance of observed cell frequencies, in 2 × 2 tables.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Developed for diagnostic odds ratios and sparse binary data; power is likely to be low, particularly when heterogeneity across studies is large.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rucker et al. arcsine transformed random-effects regression
rubrics_metrics.description: Based on an arcsine transformation to stabilise variance of binomial random variables; arcsine-transformed statistics replace variables used in Begg’s or Egger’s tests or in random-effects regression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compared with other tests, arcsine transformed random-effects regression has improved power when both effect size and heterogeneity are large. The test is relatively conservative with small sample size and in the absence of heterogeneity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trim and fill method
rubrics_metrics.description: A rank-based data augmentation technique that estimates the number of missing studies and adjusts the pooled effect by 'trimming' asymmetrical studies, estimating the funnel centre, then 'filling' with imputed counterparts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Early simulations suggested improved point estimates and CIs compared with ignoring bias, but further studies found high false-positive findings when heterogeneity is large. May spuriously adjust for bias when clinical heterogeneity exists. Use as a sensitivity analysis with caution; not definitive proof of bias or corrected effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fail-safe N (Rosenthal) and its limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Estimates the number of unpublished (null-effect) studies required to overturn a significant meta-analysis result (p < 0.05); Rosenthal suggested as 'unlikely' if greater than 5K + 10 where K is the number of published studies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Problems: overemphasises statistical significance; misleading if unpublished studies have effects in the opposite direction; interpretation depends on what number of unpublished studies is plausible; some authors (Becker) recommend abandoning the fail-safe N in favour of more informative analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weight-function sensitivity/modelling methods (Copas, Vevea & Jackson, Vevea & Woods)
rubrics_metrics.description: Selection models using weighted distribution theory: an effect-size model (distribution if no selection) plus a selection model (how selection modifies distribution). Copas and Jackson, and Vevea & Woods proposed weight-function sensitivity analyses to estimate ranges of possible bias or number of unpublished studies under different assumed selection parameters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appropriate application usually requires many studies (e.g. ~100), though Copas/Vevea methods can be used for sensitivity even with fewer studies. These should be used for sensitivity analyses (range of plausible scenarios), not to provide a single corrected estimate. Models are complex and mostly used by statistical experts; user-friendly software development is needed for mainstream use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sophisticated modelling methods (classical and Bayesian selection models)
rubrics_metrics.description: More complex approaches based on weighted distribution theory from classical or Bayesian perspectives, involving specification of effect-size and selection models.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Often require a large number of studies to apply reliably; the assumed selection processes are typically unverifiable empirically. Use primarily for sensitivity analysis; avoid treating model output as the single 'true' adjusted effect without caution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detecting outcome reporting bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Outcome reporting bias is suspected when eligible studies could not be included due to lack of outcome data. Not an issue if the outcome was not measured.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigate whether the outcome was measured: compare published reports with protocols (when available), contact study authors for unreported outcomes or clarifications. Methods include imputation (Williamson & Gamble) — which may overadjust compared with Copas methods — capture–recapture (performance not well evaluated), and excess-significance tests (Ioannidis & Trikalinos) that compare expected vs observed number of significant studies under assumptions. Use these approaches as exploratory/sensitivity assessments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fixed-effect versus random-effects model guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Fixed-effect model assumes a single true effect; random-effects assumes a distribution of effects and incorporates between-study variance. Fixed-effect weights use inverse within-study variance; random-effects use inverse total variance (within + between).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Random-effects gives relatively larger weights to smaller studies and may therefore be more vulnerable to publication bias. When heterogeneity exists, compare pooled results from both models; if random-effects pooled estimate is larger than fixed-effect estimate, investigate underlying causes (including publication bias). Be aware random-effects CIs are wider under large heterogeneity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Updating systematic reviews — when and why
rubrics_metrics.description: Updating systematic reviews can reduce the impact of publication bias because negative/less favourable results and large confirmatory trials may be published later, altering conclusions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence shows many reviews are updated and that updates can change statistical significance or effect estimates. Use priority-setting (topic/heterogeneity driven) rather than time-based updating. Shojania et al. defined quantitative signals for updating as changes in statistical significance or relative effect magnitude ≥ 50%, and qualitative signals as new information about harms or caveats affecting decision-making. Consider trial sequential analysis to adjust for increased Type I error from repeated meta-analyses, but balance against risks of Type II and other biases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of methods by stage of review
rubrics_metrics.description: Methods to handle publication bias can be classified according to the stage of a literature review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prevention before review: prospective registration of trials (trial registries) and electronic publication of trial results. Detection during review: locating unpublished studies, funnel plots and related statistical tests, sensitivity-analysis modelling. Minimising impact after review: confirmatory large-scale trials, updating the systematic review. Use appropriate method(s) at each stage rather than relying on a single post-hoc adjustment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical caveat: small numbers of studies and heterogeneity limit almost all methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Many statistical and modelling methods require a substantial number of studies and/or low heterogeneity to perform well; in practice most meta-analyses include few studies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Surveys show most meta-analyses have fewer than 10 studies and many have substantial heterogeneity. Therefore: (a) funnel-plot tests often are inappropriate or underpowered; (b) modelling approaches may be infeasible or unreliable; (c) treat all test results and model outputs as exploratory sensitivity analyses rather than definitive corrections.
